Conclusions The GeoSWAC concept benefits from two key assumptions: 1) access to an effectively infinite heat sink provided by deep seawater, and 2) a favorable natural hydraulic gradient, which enables cold seawater to rise to sea level with minimal pumping. Pumping is only required from sea level to the building infrastructure, further reducing energy demand. Functionally similar to conventional SWAC, GeoSWAC reconfigures the system vertically using inland wells instead of horizontal seabed pipelines. This design shifts constraints from ocean bathymetry to subsurface hydraulic connectivity offering potential advantages such as greater geographic flexibility and reduced sensitivity to weather during construction. However, these benefits come with uncertainties, particularly related to subsurface conditions and potential flow rate limitations due to borehole diameter constraints. Future research should focus on validating key assumptions through site-specific performance modeling, geological surveys, and feasibility-level techno- economic analysis to quantify LCOC sensitivity to these variables. This study demonstrates the potential of the GeoSWAC system as a resilient, economic, and energy-efficient alternative to electricity-intensive chiller-based cooling at a tropical, coastal university campus in Puerto Rico, based on a set of simplifying assumptions and a conceptual analysis. GeoSWAC is a concept to produce cooling through inland wells in a permeable formation hydraulically connected to deep, cold seawater. While in-depth modeling of the hydraulic connection between inland wells and deep, cold seawater in the GeoSWAC system remains for future study, economic metrics were estimated and compared with those of a water-cooled chiller system at the campus.
